summary: The specification of Datalanguage version 0/9, the language of the Datacomputer, a data storage and management utility being developed for the ARPANET. This early version is described as extremely primitive, with elementary items limited to fixed-length ASCII strings. Later versions were planned to remove that restriction.

plainLanguage.summary: Instructions for a very simple language for asking a shared storage computer to keep and fetch information for you.

subtitle: Specification of a language for describing and managing shared data storage on the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: The Datacomputer system needed a formal language to describe data structures and manage storage and retrieval operations on a shared network utility.
tldr.mechanism: Datalanguage Version 0/9 provides a syntax to define hierarchical containers (LIST for repeated items, STRUCT for grouped fields, STRING for text), and operations to create, delete, open, and transfer data, along with queries that filter by content.
tldr.outcome: An extremely primitive but functional early version of a data language; Version 0/10 and later releases were planned to add support for variable-length strings and other features.

today: RFC 515 describes an early, primitive data language that has not been obsoleted in the RFC series. The Datacomputer itself was an experimental system that did not achieve widespread adoption. The RFC notes many restrictions marked with three asterisks (***) that would be removed in Version 0/10 and beyond, such as fixed-length ASCII strings and limits on container size. The language was designed to be expanded as experience accumulated and feedback was received from early users.

sections.title: Datalanguage and the Datacomputer
sections.content:
RFC 515 specifies Datalanguage Version 0/9, the language used to communicate with the Datacomputer, a data storage and management utility being developed for the ARPANET. The Datacomputer performs storage and retrieval of data on behalf of network users, letting multiple programs share the same data without each maintaining their own copy.

Version 0/9 is described as extremely primitive: elementary data items are limited to fixed-length ASCII strings, and the language provides only basic operations. Despite these constraints, it offered early experience with data description and management concepts. Subsequent versions were planned to relax these restrictions.
sections.plainLanguage: The Datacomputer is a shared storage system on the network. Datalanguage lets you tell it what kinds of information you want to store and how to find it again.

sections.title: Containers and Structure
sections.content:
Datalanguage models all data as containers, which come in three types. A LIST holds many copies of the same kind of item (like repeated weather observations). A STRUCT is a fixed group of different fields (like a record with location and temperature). A STRING is text of a specific length.

Containers can nest: a STRUCT might contain another STRUCT and a LIST. Each container has an ident, a name by which users refer to it. Users can optionally mark a STRING field as an inversion key, which tells the Datacomputer to build an index on that field to speed up searches.
sections.plainLanguage: You describe what you want to store by saying whether each item is a list of things, a group of fields, or just text, and give each piece a name.

sections.title: Creating and Managing Data
sections.content:
Datalanguage provides operations to manage data and directories. CREATE adds a new container to the directory and allocates space. DELETE removes a container and its data. OPEN and CLOSE attach or detach a container for use. CONNECT and DISCONNECT link a port to a network address for input or output.

Assignment (the equals sign) transfers data between containers; if the containers have matching structure, their fields are paired and data moves automatically. FOR loops iterate over lists, selecting items by content using Boolean expressions (EQ, LT, GT, AND, OR, NOT) and assigning or transforming them.
sections.plainLanguage: You can create storage, delete it, open it to work with, and move data between containers, including selecting just the items you want based on their values.
